proofs.proof_tex:
Define the latent compatibility class independently of the observed-law functional \(\Theta_I(P)\).  For a fixed \(x\in\mathcal X\), call a probability law \(Q_x\) on \(\mathcal E^4\) compatible if its \((D(0),R(0))\)-margin is \(\mu_{0x}\), its \((D(1),R(1))\)-margin is \(\mu_{1x}\), and it assigns probability one to \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  The within-arm margins already obey the semicompeting-risk order by the maintained assumption.  The causal identified surface set is the collection of target surfaces induced by families \((Q_x:x\in\mathcal X)\) that, together with the observed treatment and censoring mechanisms, reproduce \(P\).  This definition precedes, and does not use, the formula defining \(\Theta_I(P)\).

First, the complete within-arm laws used below are observable-law functionals.  Positive cell support and treatment overlap give
\[
 \Pr_P(Z=z,X=x)>0
 \qquad(z\in\{0,1\},\ x\in\mathcal X),
\]
while full-horizon censoring support gives \(G_{zx}(L)\geq\gamma>0\).  Consequently every division in the IPCW identity is legal.  By the established IPCW recovery lemma, consistency, conditional exchangeability, arm-specific independent censoring, and these support conditions identify \(\mu_{zx}\), including its atom at \(\infty\).  Hence \(d_x\), \(\zeta_x\), \(b_x\), \(K_x\), \(s_x\), and \(S\) are functionals of \(P\).

We next prove necessity by a set-inclusion argument.  Let \(Q_x\) be compatible and let \(\nu_x\) be its \((D(0),R(1))\)-margin.  Its margins are \(d_x\) and \(\zeta_x\).  For every \(u\in[0,\tau]\) and every Borel \(B\subseteq\mathcal E\), terminal monotonicity gives
\[
 \{D(0)>u,R(1)\in B\}
 \subseteq
 \{D(1)>u,R(1)\in B\}.
\]
Taking \(Q_x\)-probabilities and using the treated within-arm margin yields
\[
 \nu_x((u,\infty]\times B)
 \leq \mu_{1x}((u,\infty]\times B)
 =K_x(u,B).
\]
Thus \(\nu_x\in\mathcal N_x\).  The argument uses every readmission-mark set \(B\), not merely the unmarked death-survival inequality.

For sufficiency, fix \(x\) and \(\nu_x\in\mathcal N_x\).  Put \(\alpha=\nu_x\) and \(\beta=\mu_{1x}\), both regarded as laws on \(\mathcal E^2\); they have the same second-coordinate margin \(\zeta_x\).  On two copies of \(\mathcal E^2\), introduce the closed relation
\[
 \mathcal R
 =\{((d_0,v),(d_1,v')):v=v',\ d_0\leq d_1\}.
\]
Closedness uses the closed diagonal of the compact metric space \(\mathcal E\) and the closed order graph on \([0,\tau]\sqcup\{\infty\}\).

We verify the compact-set inequalities required by the cited closed-relation coupling theorem.  The defining capacity inequality first implies its closed-tail version:
\[
 \alpha([u,\infty]\times B)\leq\beta([u,\infty]\times B)
 \qquad(u\in\mathcal E,\ B\in\mathscr B(\mathcal E)).                                      \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, for \(0<u\leq\tau\), take \(u_k\uparrow u\) with \(u_k<u\) and use continuity from above on \((u_k,\infty]\times B\).  At \(u=0\), (1) is equality because the second margins coincide.  At \(u=\infty\), it is precisely the defining inequality at the boundary cut \(u=\tau\), since \((\tau,\infty]=\{\infty\}\).  Thus neither the horizon atom nor the zero boundary is omitted.

Let \(A\subseteq\mathcal E^2\) be compact and put \(U=\mathcal R(A)\).  Compactness of \(A\) and closedness of \(\mathcal R\) on a compact product make \(U\) compact.  For each mark \(v\), the section \(U_v\) is empty or a closed upper interval \([h(v),\infty]\).  Give an empty section a separate cemetery label.  For finite \(a\),
\[
 \{v:h(v)\leq a\}
 =\operatorname{proj}_v\!left(A\cap([0,a]\times\mathcal E)\right),
\]
which is compact; hence \(h\) is Borel measurable on the nonempty sections.  Choose nested finite grids of \([0,\tau]\) with mesh decreasing to zero.  Replace every finite \(h(v)\) by the largest grid point \(\underline h_n(v)\leq h(v)\), retain the section \(\{\infty\}\) when \(h(v)=\infty\), and retain empty sections.  The resulting sets \(U_n\) decrease to \(U\).  Each \(U_n\) is a finite disjoint union of sets \([q,\infty]\times B_{nq}\), together possibly with \(\{\infty\}\times B_{n\infty}\), for Borel and pairwise disjoint mark sets \(B_{nq}\).  Summing (1) over these disjoint pieces gives \(\alpha(U_n)\leq\beta(U_n)\).  Continuity from above now gives
\[
 \alpha(A)\leq\alpha(U)leq\beta(U)=\beta(\mathcal R(A)).                                  \tag{2}
\]
The cited theorem applied to (2) supplies a coupling of \((D(0),R(1))\sim\nu_x\) and \((D(1),R'(1))\sim\mu_{1x}\) supported on \(R(1)=R'(1)\) and \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  After identifying the equal mark coordinates, denote its law on \((D(0),D(1),R(1))\) by \(\pi_x\).

It remains to attach the control readmission without altering either constructed margin.  Reorder \(\mu_{0x}\) as the law of \((R(0),D(0))\).  This law and \(\pi_x\) have the same \(D(0)\)-margin \(d_x\).  The proved compact-coordinate gluing lemma therefore gives a law \(Q_x\) of \((R(0),D(0),D(1),R(1))\) whose \((D(0),R(0))\)-margin is \(\mu_{0x}\) and whose \((D(0),D(1),R(1))\)-margin is \(\pi_x\).  It follows that
\[
 \mathcal L_{Q_x}(D(0),R(0))=\mu_{0x},\qquad
 \mathcal L_{Q_x}(D(1),R(1))=\mu_{1x},\qquad
 Q_x\{D(0)\leq D(1)\}=1.                                                               \tag{3}
\]
The strict within-arm event orders are inherited from the fixed margins \(\mu_{0x}\) and \(\mu_{1x}\).  No rank or density condition is used in this lifting step.

Because \(\mathcal X\) is finite, the cellwise collection \(x\mapsto Q_x\) is automatically a measurable probability kernel.  Draw \(X\) with masses \(p_x\); conditional on \(X=x\), draw the potential path from \(Q_x\), draw \(Z\) independently with probability \(e(x)\), and draw \(C\) from its observed conditional law given \((Z,X)\), independently of the potential path.  Apply consistency to form the factual event path.  In arm \(z\) and cell \(x\), (3) gives exactly \(\mu_{zx}\), and the construction also preserves the observed laws of \((X,Z,C)\).  Since the at-risk, terminal-event, and first-readmission histories through \(\tau\) are measurable functions of these variables, the resulting law of \(O\) is exactly \(P\).  Thus every family \(\nu_x\in\mathcal N_x\) has a measurable compatible full-law lift reproducing the observed distribution.

Finally, we calculate the causal targets under an arbitrary compatible lift.  Terminal monotonicity gives the event identity
\[
 \{D(0)>t,D(1)>t\}=\{D(0)>t\}.                                                            \tag{4}
\]
For \((r,t)\in\mathcal H_\eta\), the target-domain definition gives \(S(t)\geq\eta>0\), so conditioning and division by \(S(t)\) are valid.  Using (4), conditioning first on \(X\), and using the definitions of \(\nu_x\) and \(b_x\), we obtain
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\Pr\{R(1)\leq r\mid D(0)>t,D(1)>t\}
 -\Pr\{R(0)\leq r\mid D(0)>t,D(1)>t\}\\
 &\quad=
 \frac{\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x
 \left[\nu_x((t,\infty]\times[0,r])-b_x(r,t)\right]}{S(t)}
 =\theta_\nu(r,t).                                                                        \tag{5}
 \end{aligned}
\]
For \(0\leq a\leq t\), the pointwise identity
\[
 \min\{q,a\}=a-\int_0^a\mathbf 1\{q\leq r\}\,dr,
 \qquad q\in\mathcal E,
\]
also holds at \(q=\infty\).  The integrand is nonnegative and bounded, so Tonelli's theorem applies.  Subtracting the two conditional expectations and using (5) yields
\[
 E[\min\{R(1),a\}-\min\{R(0),a\}\mid D(0)>t,D(1)>t]
 =-\int_0^a\theta_\nu(r,t)\,dr
 =\rho_\nu(a,t).                                                                          \tag{6}
\]

Necessity shows that every monotonicity-compatible causal surface belongs to the observed-law image \(\Theta_I(P)\); the full-law construction shows that every member of that image is attained by a law satisfying all maintained restrictions and reproducing \(P\).  Equations (5)--(6) prove the relationship between the causal estimands and the observed-law functional rather than defining that relationship.  Therefore the bound is sharp---indeed, it is an exact set characterization---for the nonparametric class with \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  If terminal monotonicity is removed, both the inclusion used in necessity and the denominator identity (4) can fail, so this proof makes no equality claim for that larger class.

added_lemmas.statement: Let \(\mathsf A\) and \(\mathsf B\) be compact metric spaces, let \(\alpha\in\mathcal P(\mathsf A)\) and \(\beta\in\mathcal P(\mathsf B)\), and let \(\mathcal R\subseteq\mathsf A\times\mathsf B\) be closed.  There exists a coupling \(\pi\in\Gamma(\alpha,\beta)\) with \(\pi(\mathcal R)=1\) if and only if \(\alpha(A)\leq\beta(\mathcal R(A))\) for every compact \(A\subseteq\mathsf A\), where \(\mathcal R(A)=\{b\in\mathsf B:(a,b)\in\mathcal R\text{ for some }a\in A\}\).

added_lemmas.statement: Let \(\alpha\in\mathcal P(\mathcal E^2)\) be the law of \((A,B)\), and let \(\beta\in\mathcal P(\mathcal E^3)\) be the law of \((B',C_1,C_2)\).  If the \(B\)-margin of \(\alpha\) equals the \(B'\)-margin of \(\beta\), then there is \(\gamma\in\mathcal P(\mathcal E^4)\) whose \((A,B)\)-margin is \(\alpha\) and whose \((B,C_1,C_2)\)-margin is \(\beta\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Equip the compact metric carrier \(\mathcal E\) with a bounded compatible metric \(d\).  For every \(n\), choose a finite Borel partition \(\mathcal P_n\) that isolates \(\{\infty\}\), whose other cells have \(d\)-diameter at most \(1/n\).  Write \(\zeta\) for the common \(B\)-margin.  On \(\mathcal E^2\times\mathcal E^3\), define
\[
 \widetilde\gamma_n
 =\sum_{H\in\mathcal P_n:\,\zeta(H)>0}
 \frac{\alpha\vert_{\{B\in H\}}\otimes
       \beta\vert_{\{B'\in H\}}}{\zeta(H)}.
\]
The total mass of the summand indexed by \(H\) is \(\zeta(H)\), so \(\widetilde\gamma_n\) is a probability measure.  For every bounded measurable \(g\) on \(\mathcal E^2\),
\[
 \int g(A,B)\,d\widetilde\gamma_n
 =\sum_{H:\,\zeta(H)>0}
   \frac{\int_{\{B\in H\}}g(A,B)\,d\alpha}{\zeta(H)}
   \beta(B'\in H)
 =\int g\,d\alpha.
\]
The analogous calculation shows that the \((B',C_1,C_2)\)-margin is exactly \(\beta\).  Moreover,
\[
 d(B,B')\leq 1/n
 \quad\widetilde\gamma_n\text{-almost surely},
\]
because both coordinates lie in the same partition cell, including the isolated cell \(\{\infty\}\).

By compactness of \(\mathcal P(\mathcal E^5)\), supplied by the cited weak-compactness lemma, a subsequence converges weakly to some \(\widetilde\gamma\).  Coordinate projections are continuous, so their pushforward laws converge; since the two relevant margins are constant along the sequence, the corresponding margins of \(\widetilde\gamma\) remain \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).  The function \((b,b')\mapsto d(b,b')\) is bounded and continuous, and hence
\[
 \int d(B,B')\,d\widetilde\gamma
 =\lim_{n\to\infty}\int d(B,B')\,d\widetilde\gamma_n=0.
\]
Thus \(B=B'\) \(\widetilde\gamma\)-almost surely.  Identifying the two equal coordinates and pushing \(\widetilde\gamma\) forward to \((A,B,C_1,C_2)\) gives the asserted \(\gamma\).  This argument uses only compactness and a vanishing-mesh finite-partition limit; it invokes neither densities nor positivity.

added_lemmas.statement: In the certified three-horizon construction \(\mathfrak E_3\), the full laws represented by \(q^-_{ihj}\) and \(q^+_{ihj}\) are distinct, satisfy \(D(0)\leq D(1)\), and induce the same observable distribution because both have within-arm laws \(\mu_0^\star\) and \(\mu_1^\star\) and the same treatment and censoring mechanisms.  Nevertheless their projected couplings are \(f^-\) and \(f^+\), with \(\ell_\star(f^-)=-1/20\) and \(\ell_\star(f^+)=1/4\).  Hence every nonparametric causal model class containing both laws is non-point-identified for \(\ell_\star\) at that common observed distribution.  This upward transfer is a nonidentification statement only; it does not assert that the marked-capacity image remains sharp after terminal monotonicity is removed.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
The finite-table certificate in the strict-support proposition gives
\[
 \left(\sum_hq^-_{ihj}\right)_{ij}=f^-_{ij},\qquad
 \left(\sum_hq^+_{ihj}\right)_{ij}=f^+_{ij},\qquad
 \left(\sum_iq^-_{ihj}\right)_{hj}
 =\left(\sum_iq^+_{ihj}\right)_{hj}=\mu_{1,hj}^\star.                                    \tag{7}
\]
After attaching \(R(0)=\infty\), both laws have control margin \(\mu_0^\star\).  Every positive entry listed in the construction has \(i\leq h\), so both laws satisfy \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  They are distinct: for example,
\[
 f^-_{00}=1/10\neq1/20=f^+_{00}.                                                           \tag{8}
\]

The construction uses the same degenerate covariate, \(Z\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) independent of the potential path, and \(C=\tau=3\) under both signs.  By consistency, treatment arm \(z\) reveals only \((D(z),R(z))\).  Thus, for every measurable set \(A\) of observed paths, if \(\mathcal O(z,d,r,3)\) denotes the deterministic observed history generated from treatment \(z\), event times \((d,r)\), and censoring time \(3\), then (7) gives
\[
 \Pr_\pm(O\in A)
 =\frac12\sum_{z=0}^1
   \int\mathbf 1\{\mathcal O(z,d,r,3)\in A\}\,d\mu_z^\star(d,r),                       \tag{9}
\]
which is independent of the sign.  This also verifies conditional exchangeability directly, while \(e=1/2\) and \(G_z(u)=1\) supply treatment and full-horizon censoring overlap.

The same finite-table proposition computes
\[
 \ell_\star(f^-)=-\frac1{20},
 \qquad
 \ell_\star(f^+)=\frac14.                                                                \tag{10}
\]
Let \(\mathfrak C\) be any nonparametric causal class containing both constructed laws.  At the common observable distribution in (9), the identified set for \(\ell_\star\) over \(\mathfrak C\) contains both values in (10); by (10) they differ by \(3/10>0\).  Therefore \(\ell_\star\) is not point identified in \(\mathfrak C\).  Enlarging a model class can only add compatible full laws, so the two-law witness survives every such enlargement.  This set-inclusion argument does not show that all additional, possibly nonmonotone laws are represented by \(\mathcal N_x\), and accordingly proves no enlarged-class sharpness claim.
added_lemmas.justification: The two-law certificate transfers nonidentification to every larger causal class containing the certified lifts without falsely transferring sharpness of the monotonicity-restricted capacity image.
added_lemmas.gap: A strict support calculation inside the monotone class does not by itself say what survives when that class is enlarged; equality of the induced observed laws supplies the required upward-transfer witness.
added_lemmas.consumer: Applied users who decline terminal monotonicity still obtain a certified nonidentification conclusion, but not the monotonicity-restricted sharp capacity characterization.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed: For the TV-SACE and RM-SACE estimands of Comment et al., among all nonparametric full laws that reproduce \(P\) and satisfy the maintained restrictions, including the additional audited restriction \(D(0)\leq D(1)\), the set of resulting standardized surface pairs is exactly \(\Theta_I(P)\).  Necessity follows from the readmission-specific survivor-capacity inequalities, and every measurable family \(\nu_x\in\mathcal N_x\) admits a measurable full-law lift of \((D(0),R(0),D(1),R(1))\) that preserves \(\mu_{0x}\) and \(\mu_{1x}\), satisfies \(D(0)\leq D(1)\), and reproduces \(P\).  Thus \(\Theta_I(P)\) is sharp for the monotonicity-restricted nonparametric class.  No equality with \(\Theta_I(P)\) is asserted for a larger class that drops terminal monotonicity.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The earlier wording could be read as maximal over Comment et al.'s unrestricted nonmonotone class. That class does not impose the exact condition \(D(0)\le D(1)\); without it, the marked-survivor set inclusion and the always-survivor denominator identity both fail. The repaired scope is a subclass of the unrestricted nonparametric causal class and is generally incomparable with Comment et al.'s fitted shared-frailty family.

Theorem 7 characterizes existence of a probability measure with prescribed marginals under support inequalities.
Characterizes sharp bounds for continuous functionals of latent joint potential-outcome laws through random-set inequalities and linear programs.

prose_updates.tldr: Death truncates readmission, so the two-index TV-SACE and RM-SACE surfaces depend on an unidentified cross-world assignment of treated readmission times to control death times. Under arm-specific independent censoring through the full horizon and the additional maintained order \(D(0)\le D(1)\), the note characterizes the complete sharp monotonicity-restricted surface by a necessary-and-sufficient marked-capacity lift, proves common fixed-cohort extremizers and exact RM integration, and gives a certified three-horizon law whose joint cross-cohort support is strictly narrower than its coordinate rectangle. Quadratic chain flows, qualitative continuous-grid convergence, and deterministic-grid finite-sample outer containment make the population characterization computable. A joint marked-product-limit/IPCW functional limit, root-\(n\) grid-bias control, and simultaneous multiplier bands remain open.

project_justification.gap: Comment et al. define clinically meaningful TV-SACE and RM-SACE surfaces but leave their cross-world law to a parametric illness--death shared-frailty model and do not impose terminal monotonicity. Existing scalar or fixed-stratum bounds and generic transport formulations do not establish the complete readmission-specific capacity inequalities or a measurable lift for the changing always-survivor surface.
project_justification.niche: After separately auditing the additional restriction \(D(0)\le D(1)\), each always-survivor cohort becomes a nested marked-resource selection problem. This yields a nonparametric sharp class that is a subclass of the unrestricted causal model but generally incomparable with Comment et al.'s fitted shared-frailty family.
project_justification.fill: The note proves the monotonicity-restricted if-and-only-if capacity image, constructive full-law sharpness, common fixed-cohort extremizers, exact RM integration, a certified strict cross-cohort support example, quadratic computation, qualitative continuous approximation, and deterministic-grid finite-sample outer containment. The certified pair of observationally equivalent monotone lifts also proves nonidentification in every larger class containing them, without claiming that the capacity image remains sharp there.

prose_updates.related_work: Comment, Mealli, Haneuse, and Zigler (2025) define the TV-SACE and RM-SACE estimands and estimate them with a Bayesian illness--death shared-frailty model. The present equality is instead a sharp nonparametric characterization after adding the audited restriction \(D(0)\le D(1)\); it is not an equality result for their unrestricted nonmonotone causal class, and their fitted shared-frailty family is generally incomparable with this monotonicity-restricted nonparametric class. Yang and Ding (2018) use detailed survival histories and copula sensitivity without monotonicity for scalar SACE bounds, which does not determine the nested compatible surface. Nevo and Gorfine (2022) study semi-competing-risk bounds under a single population stratification. Chen, Cui, and Yang (2024) transform fixed-time SACE programs and integrate scalar bounds but do not prove common changing-cohort surface extremizers. Strassen (1965) supplies the closed-relation coupling criterion; the readmission-marked cut reduction and full four-time lift are proved here. Russell (2021), Ober-Reynolds (2023), and Gao, Ge, and Qian (2024) motivate generic latent-law and transport programs, whereas the quadratic nested chain is specific to the maintained terminal order. Goldberg (2019) supplies standard IPCW recovery and concentration tools. Cho and Russell (2024), Bluhmki et al. (2019), Fang and Santos (2019), and Firpo, Galvao, and Parker (2023) inform the still-open simultaneous-inference route.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The marked-capacity image is proved sharp only over nonparametric full laws satisfying the maintained terminal-monotonicity restriction \(D(0)\le D(1)\), in addition to the stated exchangeability, event-order, overlap, and full-horizon censoring conditions. It is not asserted to equal the identified set in Comment et al.'s unrestricted nonmonotone class; without monotonicity, marked-capacity necessity and the denominator reduction can fail. The two certified monotone lifts remain an observational-equivalence and nonidentification witness in any larger class containing them, but this does not transfer capacity sharpness. The joint marked-process functional central limit theorem, estimated-censoring expansion, root-\(n\)-negligible grid bias, and simultaneous multiplier validity remain open.

statement_notes.justification: This is the theorem-level kernel: it gives the exact nonparametric surface image under the separately audited terminal-monotonicity restriction, rather than extending that equality to an unrestricted nonmonotone class.
statement_notes.gap: Comment et al. define the estimands under a generally nonmonotone causal setup and fit a shared-frailty model; neither their model nor generic transport results prove the readmission-specific capacity equivalence and full-law lift for the monotonicity-restricted nonparametric class.
statement_notes.consumer: Clinicians obtain every TV-SACE/RM-SACE conclusion implied by the observed law and maintained terminal monotonicity; if that order is not credible, the three-horizon corollary still certifies nonidentification but the capacity equality is not claimed.

proofs.proof_tex:
We give an exact finite-table certificate and then a smoothing construction.  All probabilities in the finite calculation are conditional on the sole value of \(X\), so the covariate subscript can be suppressed.

First consider the primitive exhibit \(\mathfrak E_3\).  Because \(R(0)=\infty\), the control numerator in the definition of the TV-SACE surface is
\[
b(r,t)=\Pr\{R(0)\le r,D(0)>t\}=0
\]
at every finite \(r\).  The four control death rows each have mass \(1/4\); hence
\[
S(1)=\frac34,\qquad S(2)=\frac12,\qquad S(3)=\frac14.
\]
Thus \(0<\eta\le 1/4\) puts \((1,1),(2,2),(3,3)\) in \(\mathcal H_\eta\), including the boundary case \(S(3)=\eta=1/4\).

Write \(f=(f_{ij})\) for an arbitrary feasible projected coupling and define the three unstandardized treated numerators
\[
A_1=\sum_{i>0}f_{i0},\qquad
A_2=\sum_{\substack{i>1\\j\le1}}f_{ij},\qquad
A_3=\sum_{j\le2}f_{3j}.
\]
The singleton marked-capacity inequalities in the grid characterization give
\[
A_1\le\kappa^\star_{00}=\frac15.
\]
Since the total demand in rows \(i>0\) is \(3/4\), while the other three marked tails across the first death cut have total capacity
\[
\kappa^\star_{01}+\kappa^\star_{02}+\kappa^\star_{03}
=\frac15+\frac3{20}+\frac7{20}=\frac7{10},
\]
the same inequalities also give
\[
A_1
=\frac34-\sum_{j=1}^3\sum_{i>0}f_{ij}
\ge\frac34-\frac7{10}=\frac1{20}.
\]
At the second death cut,
\[
A_2\le\kappa^\star_{10}+\kappa^\star_{11}
=\frac3{20}+\frac1{10}=\frac14.
\]
The total mass in rows \(i>1\) is \(1/2\), and the capacity available in columns \(2,3\) across that cut is \(3/20+3/10=9/20\).  Consequently
\[
A_2
=\frac12-\sum_{j=2}^3\sum_{i>1}f_{ij}
\ge\frac12-\frac9{20}=\frac1{20}.
\]
Finally, the third-cut capacities and the last-row demand imply
\[
A_3\le\kappa^\star_{20}+\kappa^\star_{21}+\kappa^\star_{22}
=\frac1{10}+\frac1{20}+\frac1{20}=\frac15
\]
and
\[
A_3=\frac14-f_{33}\ge\frac14-\kappa^\star_{23}
=\frac14-\frac15=\frac1{20}.
\]

These six inequalities are sharp.  The displayed flow \(f^+\) attains the upper endpoints for \(A_1\) and \(A_3\), whereas \(f^-\) attains the upper endpoint for \(A_2\) and the lower endpoint for \(A_3\).  For the two remaining lower endpoints, consider the arrays
\[
100g^{(1)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
20&0&0&5\\
0&15&5&5\\
0&0&5&20\\
5&5&5&10
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
100g^{(2)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
20&0&0&5\\
0&20&0&5\\
0&0&10&15\\
5&0&5&15
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Both have row sums \((25,25,25,25)/100\) and column sums \((25,20,15,40)/100\).  Their complete singleton chain loads, again multiplied by \(100\), are
\[
\left(\sum_{i>k}g^{(1)}_{ij}\right)_{kj}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
5&20&15&35\\
5&5&10&30\\
5&5&5&10
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\left(\sum_{i>k}g^{(2)}_{ij}\right)_{kj}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
5&20&15&35\\
5&0&15&30\\
5&0&5&15
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Each entry is no larger than the corresponding entry of \(100\kappa^\star\).  Hence both arrays are feasible by \(\mathrm{thm{:}quadratic\text{-}chain\text{-}flow}\); \(g^{(1)}\) has \(A_1=1/20\), and \(g^{(2)}\) has \(A_2=1/20\).  The feasible flow set is convex because its margins are affine equalities and its capacities and nonnegativity restrictions are linear inequalities.  The image of that set under each linear map \(f\mapsto A_j\) is therefore an interval, and the endpoint constructions prove
\[
A_1\in\left[\frac1{20},\frac15\right],\qquad
A_2\in\left[\frac1{20},\frac14\right],\qquad
A_3\in\left[\frac1{20},\frac15\right].
\]
Dividing by the strictly positive survivor masses displayed above, as required by the definition of \(\theta_\nu\), yields the exact coordinate intervals
\[
\theta_\nu(1,1)\in\left[\frac1{15},\frac4{15}\right],\qquad
\theta_\nu(2,2)\in\left[\frac1{10},\frac12\right],\qquad
\theta_\nu(3,3)\in\left[\frac15,\frac45\right].
\]

We next verify the two claimed full-law lifts.  Direct summation of the nonzero entries specified in the definition gives
\[
100\left(\sum_hq^-_{ihj}\right)_{ij}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
10&0&10&5\\
0&10&5&10\\
15&5&0&5\\
0&5&0&20
\end{pmatrix}
=100f^-,
\]
\[
100\left(\sum_hq^+_{ihj}\right)_{ij}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
5&0&10&10\\
10&15&0&0\\
0&0&0&25\\
10&5&5&5
\end{pmatrix}
=100f^+,
\]
and, for both signs,
\[
100\left(\sum_iq^\pm_{ihj}\right)_{hj}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
5&0&0&5\\
5&10&0&5\\
5&5&10&10\\
10&5&5&20
\end{pmatrix}
=100\mu_1^\star.
\]
Every listed entry is nonnegative.  The first two displays prove the asserted \((D(0),R(1))\) margins, and the third proves the treated \((D(1),R(1))\) margin.  Summing either \(f^\pm\) across its readmission columns gives the control death margin \((1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4)\).  After setting \(R(0)=\infty\), this is exactly \(\mu_0^\star\).  Inspection of every listed positive triple gives \(i\le h\), so its support satisfies \(D(0)\le D(1)\).  The positive cells of \(\mu_1^\star\) also have \(r_j^\star<d_h^\star\) whenever \(r_j^\star<\infty\), and the control order is vacuous because \(R(0)=\infty\).  Thus both lifts obey the semicompeting-risk order.

For completeness, the row sums and column sums of \(f^\pm\) are respectively
\[
\left(\frac14,\frac14,\frac14,\frac14\right)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\left(\frac14,\frac15,\frac3{20},\frac25\right).
\]
Their singleton chain-load matrices are those displayed in the definition and are entrywise bounded by \(\kappa^\star\).  On this finite ordered support, every threshold \(u\) induces either one of the three nontrivial death cuts or a trivial cut.  Every Borel readmission-mark set induces a subset of the four atoms, and summing the valid singleton-column inequalities proves the inequality for that subset.  Hence the displayed checks certify all event-set capacity restrictions, not merely prefix restrictions.

We now calculate the genuinely joint support.  Substitution of \(S(1)=3/4\), \(S(2)=1/2\), \(S(3)=1/4\) into the signed direction gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_\star(\nu)
&=\sum_{i>0}f_{i0}
  -\sum_{\substack{i>1\\j\le1}}f_{ij}
  +\sum_{j\le2}f_{3j}\\
&=f_{10}-f_{21}+f_{30}+f_{32}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the upper endpoint, nonnegativity and the first and third cut capacities imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_\star(\nu)
&\le f_{10}+f_{30}+f_{32}\\
&\le \sum_{i>0}f_{i0}+\sum_{i>2}f_{i2}\\
&\le\kappa^\star_{00}+\kappa^\star_{22}
=\frac15+\frac1{20}=\frac14.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the lower endpoint, the second-cut capacity in column \(1\) and the last-row margin give
\[
f_{21}+f_{31}\le\kappa^\star_{11}=\frac1{10},
\qquad
f_{30}+f_{31}+f_{32}
=\frac14-f_{33}
\ge\frac14-\kappa^\star_{23}=\frac1{20}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_\star(\nu)
&=f_{10}-(f_{21}+f_{31})+(f_{30}+f_{31}+f_{32})\\
&\ge 0-\frac1{10}+\frac1{20}=-\frac1{20}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Direct substitution in the displayed flows gives
\[
\ell_\star(f^-)=-\frac1{20},
\qquad
\ell_\star(f^+)=\frac14.
\]
The full lifts already verified show that both endpoints are attainable under terminal monotonicity.  Convex mixing of the two full laws preserves both within-arm margins and every maintained structural restriction, so every intermediate value is attainable.  Thus the sharp signed support is exactly
\[
\left[-\frac1{20},\frac14\right].
\]

If the three coordinates could instead be varied independently over their exact marginal intervals, the smallest and largest values in the same signed direction would be
\[
\frac34\frac1{15}-\frac12\frac12+\frac14\frac15
=-\frac3{20}
\]
and
\[
\frac34\frac4{15}-\frac12\frac1{10}+\frac14\frac45
=\frac7{20},
\]
respectively.  Hence the coordinate rectangle has support interval
\[
\left[-\frac3{20},\frac7{20}\right],
\]
which strictly contains the sharp joint interval, with a gap \(1/10\) at each endpoint.

It remains to show that the certificate is compatible with the regularity assumptions and is not an atomic knife-edge example.  Choose a nonnegative symmetric continuously differentiable density \(\varphi_\delta\), of integral one and support contained in \((-\delta,\delta)\), where \(0<\delta<1/8\).  Replace every finite category by the corresponding translate of this density and leave the atom at \(\infty\) unchanged.  Conditional on a positive categorical lift cell \((i,h,j)\), use independent translated bump draws for the two finite death coordinates when \(i<h\), use the same death draw when \(i=h\), and take the readmission bump draw independently.  If a coordinate has category \(\infty\), leave it equal to \(\infty\).

This construction preserves every categorical mass in both within-arm margins.  If \(i<h\), adjacent finite death centers are one unit apart, so \(\delta<1/8\) implies \(D(0)<D(1)\); if \(i=h\), the shared draw implies \(D(0)=D(1)\).  The smallest gap between a finite treated readmission center and a compatible treated death center is \(1/4\).  Therefore
\[
\sup R(1)\le r_j^\star+\delta
<d_h^\star-\delta\le\inf D(1)
\]
inside every cell with finite readmission, because \(2\delta<1/4\).  The semicompeting order is thus preserved.  Finite-part marginal densities are finite mixtures of translates of \(\varphi_\delta\), and finite-part joint densities are finite mixtures of products of such translates.  They consequently have finite sup-norm and Lipschitz constants; choosing \(M\) and \(L_{\mathrm{Lip}}\) no smaller than these finite constants verifies the two density conditions.

The supports of the death bumps do not cross the integer thresholds \(1,2,3\), and the supports of the readmission bumps do not cross the corresponding readmission thresholds.  Consequently every indicator entering \(A_1,A_2,A_3\), every survivor denominator, and every capacity inequality used above has exactly its categorical value.  Conversely, every admissible smoothed full law projects at these thresholds to a categorical flow satisfying the same necessary capacity inequalities.  For attainability, apply the full-law lift part of \(\mathrm{thm{:}quadratic\text{-}chain\text{-}flow}\) to each categorical endpoint flow and then apply the preceding shared-bump construction to that lift.  Thus the six coordinate endpoints and the two signed endpoints remain attainable, and all the exact support calculations above remain valid for the smoothed law.

The remaining maintained sampling conditions hold explicitly: \(X\) is degenerate with positive mass, \(Z\) is independent of all potential variables with \(e=1/2\), factual outcomes are assigned by consistency, and \(C=\tau=3\) gives
\[
G_{zx}(u)=1\ge\gamma\qquad(0\le u\le\tau).
\]
In particular, censoring support is verified through the full analysis horizon rather than only before the last event.

Finally, keep the separated bump kernels and their structural incidence pattern fixed and vary their finitely many mixture weights within the feasible parameter cone.  The relevant coordinate and signed support problems then have a fixed finite constraint matrix, with the mixture weights entering only the right-hand side.  After slack variables are added, there are finitely many possible bases.  On the relative region where any one basis is feasible and optimal, its basic solution and its objective are affine functions of the weights; where optimality regions meet, their objective values agree.  The endpoint maps are therefore continuous and piecewise affine on this finite polyhedral parameter cone.  At the displayed law both strict gaps equal \(1/10\), so continuity leaves both gaps positive throughout a sufficiently small relatively open neighborhood of the smoothed law.  This proves the asserted robust strict cross-cohort separation within the maintained monotonicity-restricted model.

added_lemmas.statement: The two monotone full laws in \(\mathfrak E_3\) constructed from \(q^-_{ihj}\) and \(q^+_{ihj}\), with \(R(0)=\infty\), the common randomized treatment mechanism, and \(C=3\), induce the same observed-data law \(P\).  Both satisfy \(D(0)\le D(1)\), but their values of \(\ell_\star\) are \(-1/20\) and \(1/4\), respectively.  Consequently \(\ell_\star\), and hence the joint pair \((\theta_\nu,\rho_\nu)\), is not point identified in any nonparametric causal model class containing both laws.  This upward nonidentification implication does not assert that \(\Theta_I(P)\) remains sharp after the maintained terminal-monotonicity class is enlarged.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
By \(\mathrm{prop{:}strict\text{-}cross\text{-}cohort\text{-}support}\), both arrays are probability laws supported on \(D(0)\le D(1)\), both have control within-arm margin \(\mu_0^\star\) after \(R(0)=\infty\) is attached, and both have treated within-arm margin \(\mu_1^\star\).  The construction of \(\mathfrak E_3\) uses in both cases the same degenerate distribution of \(X\), the same independent treatment law \(\Pr(Z=1)=1/2\), and the same censoring time \(C=3\).  Under consistency, conditional on \(Z=z\) the observed pair \((D,R)\) has law \(\mu_z^\star\).  Hence, for every measurable set \(A\) in the observed path space,
\[
\Pr(O\in A)
=\frac12\Pr_{\mu_0^\star}\{O(0)\in A\}
 +\frac12\Pr_{\mu_1^\star}\{O(1)\in A\},
\]
where the at-risk and event-history components of \(O(z)\) are deterministic measurable functions of \((D(z),R(z),C,z,X)\).  The right-hand side is identical for the two full laws, proving that they induce the same \(P\).

The same proposition gives their distinct attained values
\[
\ell_\star=-\frac1{20}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\ell_\star=\frac14.
\]
Thus the two full laws are observationally equivalent but disagree on a linear functional of the TV-SACE surface.  They therefore disagree on the joint surface pair as well, irrespective of the deterministic RM relation \(\rho_\nu(a,t)=-\int_0^a\theta_\nu(r,t)\,dr\).  If a larger nonparametric causal class contains both laws, the same pair remains an observational-equivalence witness inside that class, so point identification fails there.  This containment argument transfers only nonidentification upward: once terminal monotonicity or another maintained restriction is removed, it supplies neither necessity nor sufficiency of the marked-capacity fiber and therefore does not establish sharpness of \(\Theta_I(P)\) for the enlarged class.
